overview: The map’s medieval Moldova means the principality usually called Moldavia in English. It was not the modern Republic of Moldova. The imported outline is misleading: it omits Suceava and much of the principality’s historical western territory. Suceava’s fortress and town were major centres of princely government, craft production and household life during the fifteenth century.

periods.title: A fifteenth-century view of Moldavia
periods.summary: This map interval covers part of the principality’s history; its rulers and institutions continued beyond 1492.

sections.title: Homes with a decorated source of warmth

items.text: Archaeologists at Suceava identified fifteenth-century houses built from wood covered with clay. Some stood on stone foundations, and some had cellars. Ordinary construction materials can leave clues even when the wooden building itself has disappeared.

Tile stoves were a recurring feature of the fifteenth-century town’s houses. Some tiles were simple, while others carried elaborate Gothic decoration. A source of indoor warmth could also be a large decorative feature, rather like furniture that happened to heat the room.

Workshops stood among homes rather than in a completely separate industrial district. Excavations identified jewellery-making, bronze-working and bone-working near residences. Richer houses and modest dwellings also occurred alongside one another, complicating a simple picture of separate rich and poor neighbourhoods.

sections.title: Money with a name and an animal

items.text: Under Stephen the Great, who ruled from 1457 to 1504, the Suceava mint produced silver groși and half-groși. Coins excavated at Orheiul Vechi include his issues. Their designs combine the ruler’s name, a shield and an aurochs head with other heraldic symbols.

A typeI coin legend reads “MONETA MOLDAVIE”, Latin for “money of Moldavia”. The museum transcribes it beside the aurochs-head design. Scholars disagree about the exact issuing dates, but the proposed typeI ranges fall within Stephen’s early reign, between 1457 and 1476.

A charter dated 17 March 1492 confirmed villages held by Şteful and his sister Marina after they lost the document inherited from their grandfather. Even a medieval family could face the dreaded missing-paperwork problem. Here, a replacement record protected a brother’s and sister’s property claim.

Other surviving documents record gifts by the treasurer Iuga to Putna Monastery in 1476. Such records connect named officials, religious institutions and property. Donations were also transactions that people wanted written down and remembered.

A 2022 exhibition assembled forty-one documents issued by Stephen’s chancery between 1458 and 1503, plus Iuga’s three records. Most were issued at Suceava, with others at Vaslui, Iași or Bădeuți. Their dates and places let historians follow a government operating through several princely residences.

Suceava’s late-fourteenth-century fortress remained a principal residence of Moldavian rulers for almost two hundred years. Surviving carved stonework records building methods and decoration, including Gothic themes prominent in the fifteenth century. Government required rooms and skilled builders as well as rulers.

Late-fourteenth- and early-fifteenth-century Moldavian churches could be decorated with ceramic discs, cross-shaped floral pieces and bricks, some glazed. These elements formed coloured bands around windows and beneath roofs. Fired clay contributed to the appearance of important public buildings as well as domestic heating.

Siret’s Holy Trinity Church preserves this kind of ceramic architectural decoration. Archaeological fragments also come from Suceava, Cetatea Albă, old monasteries and other settlements. Comparing intact buildings with excavated pieces helps researchers reconstruct decorative traditions that no longer survive everywhere.

The oldest surviving bells assigned to the medieval Moldavian state date from Stephen the Great’s reign. Bells can preserve inscriptions, decorations and coats of arms as well as producing sound. They are material records of the people and institutions that commissioned them.

ending.text: Moldavia did not disappear in 1492. Much later, the 1859 election of Alexandru Ioan Cuza in both Moldavia and Wallachia began their union, leading toward the modern Romanian state.
